18894:
Baptism was understood as a decisive washing away of sins. So what if a baptised Christian then committed adultery, murder or denied Christ under persecution? Hebrews seemed to say renewal was impossible for those who fall away. Different leaders answered differently.

The Shepherd of Hermas (Rome, second century) taught that there is one further repentance available after baptism, but only one. Tertullian, in *On Repentance* (about 203), described a public, humiliating 'second repentance' (exomologesis) with sackcloth and fasting. Later, as a Montanist, he attacked a bishop who forgave adultery after penance, in *On Modesty*.

After the Decian persecution (250) the question became urgent: many had lapsed. Cyprian of Carthage allowed the lapsed back after penance; Novatian at Rome refused and formed a stricter rival church. The mainstream church chose the path of disciplined mercy. Public penance, usually allowed once in a lifetime, became the norm, which is one reason many delayed baptism.
18895: Whose edict Tertullian attacked in On Modesty is disputed: older scholars said Callistus of Rome, many now think a bishop of Carthage, possibly Agrippinus. The underlying dispute, whether the church may forgive grave sins after baptism, is clear.
18896: Augustine: restless hearts and disordered desire
18897:
Augustine's *Confessions* (about 397–400) is the first great Christian autobiography of an inner life. He traces his sins back to infancy, describes a will divided against itself, and tells of his conversion in a Milan garden on reading Paul's call to put on Christ rather than gratify the flesh.

In his controversy with Pelagius (from 411), Augustine argued that all humans inherit Adam's guilt and a disordered desire he called concupiscence, a craving that pulls the will toward lesser goods, especially visible in sexual desire. Without God's grace no one can even begin to love God rightly. Pelagius, a British monk, held that God commands only what we can do and called Christians to strenuous moral effort. The church sided with Augustine at Carthage in 418.

The Greek East did not adopt Augustine's view of inherited guilt. It tended to describe the human problem as mortality and passions, a sickness that Christ heals. In the West, Augustine's picture of the divided self shaped preaching on sin for over a thousand years.
18898: Myth: 'Augustine invented original sin.' Correction: earlier writers including Tertullian, Cyprian and Ambrose spoke of humanity's inherited fallenness and baptised infants for the remission of sin. Augustine sharpened and systematised the idea, especially the notion of inherited guilt.
18900:
From the sixth century Irish monks spread private, repeatable confession. Penitentials listed sins with matching penances, for example so many days of fasting for a particular fault. The seven deadly sins (pride, envy, anger, sloth, greed, gluttony, lust), developed from Evagrius and Cassian and fixed by Gregory the Great, gave preachers and confessors a framework.

In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council required all Christians to confess at least once a year to their own priest. Confessors' manuals multiplied, teaching priests how to question penitents about every area of life. Preaching friars urged hearers to examine themselves, feel contrition and make satisfaction. Mystics such as Bernard of Clairvaux and later Thomas a Kempis's *Imitation of Christ* called for inward holiness and love.

Historians differ on the result. Some, like Thomas Tentler, see a 'social control' that bred anxiety; others, like Eamon Duffy, stress the comfort and community of sacramental life. Both agree that sin had become something to be examined, named and dealt with regularly by each individual.
18902:
Martin Luther, as an Augustinian friar, confessed for hours and still felt no peace: he could never be sure he had confessed everything or felt enough sorrow. He later described hating the phrase 'the righteousness of God' because he heard it as God's punishing justice, until he came to see it in Romans 1:17 as the righteousness God gives to faith. The date of this breakthrough is debated (between about 1514 and 1519).

Luther's experience shaped Protestant preaching. The law's job is to terrify the conscience and show the sinner's helplessness; the gospel's job is to comfort with God's free promise in Christ. The believer is at the same time righteous (in Christ) and a sinner (in themselves). Holiness follows as fruit of faith, not as a condition of acceptance.

Catholics replied at Trent that justification includes real inner renewal and that Luther's view risked neglecting holiness. Lutherans and Reformed Christians replied that good works flow from faith and that only a gift can bring peace to a conscience.
18904:
English Puritans wanted a church and a heart fully reformed. William Perkins and others wrote 'cases of conscience' and mapped the steps of conversion. Because Reformed theology taught that the elect would show signs of grace, believers searched their lives for evidence: diaries, self-examination before communion, and pastoral counsel on assurance. This produced deep spiritual literature, and for some sensitive souls, deep anxiety.

John Wesley added a different note. After his Aldersgate experience (1738) he preached that believers could receive assurance from the Spirit and could be made perfect in love: not sinless in every sense, but freed from wilful sin so that love for God and neighbour fills the heart. Methodist societies held members to account in small 'class meetings' and General Rules that forbade, for example, drunkenness and fighting.

Calvinists criticised Christian perfection as unrealistic; Wesleyans replied that Scripture commands holiness and God's grace is strong enough. Both put personal holiness at the centre of the evangelical life.
18906:
In nineteenth-century America, Phoebe Palmer taught a 'shorter way' to holiness: lay everything on the altar in consecration, believe God's promise, and receive entire sanctification as a distinct experience. The holiness movement that followed produced new denominations and fed directly into Pentecostalism.

In Britain the Keswick Convention (from 1875) offered a gentler 'higher life': not sinless perfection, but victory over known sin through surrender and faith, letting Christ live his life in the believer. Hannah Whitall Smith's *The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life* (1875) popularised it. Phrases like 'let go and let God' became associated with the movement.

Critics such as B. B. Warfield and later J. I. Packer argued that Keswick teaching created two classes of Christians and encouraged passivity, whereas Scripture calls for active, lifelong struggle. Defenders reply that it gave weary Christians real freedom and rightly stressed dependence on God.
18907: Fundamentalist codes and modern grace movements
18908:
In the early twentieth century, holiness often became defined by separation from 'worldly amusements'. Many fundamentalist and holiness churches forbade drinking, smoking, dancing, card-playing and cinema, and some regulated dress. Historians such as George Marsden and Joel Carpenter note that these codes marked the boundary between the church and a culture seen as drifting from God. They also gave communities clear identity and protected many families from real harms, though critics saw legalism and a focus on outward behaviour.

From the late twentieth century, reaction set in. The 'Lordship salvation' controversy (1988–89) pitted John MacArthur, who insisted saving faith includes submission to Christ, against Zane Hodges, who held that faith alone saves even without visible fruit. More recently 'grace' preachers such as Joseph Prince stress that believers are already wholly forgiven and should not dwell on sin. Critics, including Michael Brown, call this 'hyper-grace' and warn it neglects repentance.

Earlier voices frame this whole debate. Dietrich Bonhoeffer warned against 'cheap grace', forgiveness without discipleship. Dallas Willard criticised a 'gospel of sin management' that deals with guilt but leaves life unchanged.
18909: Stendahl and the 'introspective conscience of the West'
18910:
In a famous 1963 essay, Swedish New Testament scholar Krister Stendahl argued that the West had read Paul through Augustine and Luther. Their agonised question, how can I find a gracious God, was not Paul's. Paul had a 'robust conscience': he called himself blameless under the law and showed little guilt. His real concern in Romans and Galatians was how Gentiles could belong to God's people without becoming Jews. Romans 7, Stendahl argued, is about the law, not a portrait of Paul's anguished soul.

The essay helped launch what James Dunn in 1982 named the 'New Perspective on Paul', alongside E. P. Sanders' argument that first-century Judaism was not a religion of earning salvation. It encouraged preachers to stress community, Jew-Gentile unity and God's covenant faithfulness.

Critics, such as Stephen Westerholm and Frank Thielman, reply that Paul does describe universal guilt (Romans 1–3), that justification addresses individuals before God, and that Luther's reading captures something real even if his experience differed from Paul's. Some point out that Augustine's *Confessions* shows the introspective conscience long before Luther, which fits Stendahl's point about the West but not his dating of the problem to the Reformation alone.
18911: Does Romans 7:14-25 describe Paul's experience as a Christian (Augustine's later view, Luther, Calvin), Paul before conversion (many early Greek fathers, and many modern scholars), or Israel's or Adam's experience under the law in the first person (Stendahl, Moo in part, Wright)? The answer shapes how preachers talk about the struggle with sin.

18999: What the Early Church Believed About Life After Death
19000: What did the first Christians believe happens when you die, and how did they think it would all end?
19001: The earliest Christians did not mainly hope for their souls to float off to heaven forever. Their great hope was the resurrection: on the last day God would raise the dead bodily, as he had raised Jesus, and renew the world. In between death and resurrection, most believed the dead wait in a conscious 'holding' state, called Hades, paradise or Abraham's bosom, with martyrs often thought to go straight to Christ. They believed Christ himself had gone down to the realm of the dead, they prayed for and remembered the departed, and they argued hard with Greek thinkers who prized the soul but despised the body. Over time the two ideas, an immortal soul and a raised body, were woven together into the classic Christian picture.
19002: The central early hope was bodily resurrection on the last day, not the soul's escape from the body.
19003: Most early writers taught an 'intermediate state': the dead are conscious and waiting, not yet in their final condition.
19004: Martyrs were widely believed to enter Christ's presence at once, which gave their deaths huge meaning for the churches.
19005: Christ's descent to the dead (later called the 'harrowing of hell') is attested early, in the second century, not first in the Middle Ages.
19006: Christians prayed for and remembered the dead from at least about AD 200, though this did not yet mean the later doctrine of purgatory.
19007: Greek ideas of the soul's immortality were both resisted and borrowed; the result was a synthesis, not a simple takeover.
19008: The starting point: Jewish hope and Jesus' resurrection
19009:
Christianity was born inside a Judaism that was divided about the afterlife. The older scriptures mostly picture the dead going down to Sheol, a shadowy place of silence (Ps 6:5, Eccl 9:10). Later texts speak of a coming day when 'many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake' (Dan 12:2). By Jesus' time Pharisees affirmed resurrection, while Sadducees denied it (Acts 23:6-8, Matt 22:23-32).

The first Christians took the Pharisees' side, but with a twist nobody expected. They claimed that one man, Jesus, had already been raised ahead of everyone else, as the 'firstfruits' of a coming harvest (1 Cor 15:20-23). Resurrection was not just a future doctrine; it had started.

This is why early Christian hope looked forward to a body, not away from one. Paul says the resurrection body will be different, 'spiritual' and imperishable, but still a body (1 Cor 15:42-44). His hope is not to be 'unclothed' but 'further clothed' (2 Cor 5:1-4), and he expects Christ to transform 'our lowly body' to be like his glorious body (Phil 3:20-21).
19010: Myth: 'Early Christians believed that when you die your soul goes to heaven, and that is the final goal.' Correction: for the earliest writers, going to be 'with Christ' at death (Phil 1:23) was real but temporary. The goal was resurrection and a renewed creation. The creeds confess 'the resurrection of the body' (Apostles' Creed) and 'the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come' (Nicene Creed, 381), not simply 'the soul going to heaven'.
19011: Resurrection of the flesh: why the body mattered so much
19012:
In the second century, Christians had to defend bodily resurrection on two fronts. Pagan critics found it disgusting or absurd: why would anyone want a corpse back? Some Christian groups, often called Gnostics, agreed with the critics and taught that only the spirit is saved.

Mainstream writers answered firmly. Clement of Rome (around AD 96) points to day and night and seeds rising from the earth as pictures of resurrection. Justin Martyr argues that the God who formed a human from a tiny seed can certainly raise a body again. The Martyrdom of Polycarp has the old bishop praying to share in 'the resurrection to eternal life, both of soul and body.' Irenaeus of Lyon devotes much of book five of *Against Heresies* to the claim that the flesh, which God made and Christ took on, is capable of salvation. Tertullian wrote a whole treatise titled *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, around 208.

The point was not only about the future. If God would raise the body, then the body is good, creation is good, and what Christians did with their bodies mattered now. That is how the early writers connected the resurrection with sexual ethics, care for the poor and sick, and burial of the dead.
19013: When Paul preached the resurrection in Athens, some listeners mocked (Acts 17:32). The second-century pagan Celsus later called the Christian hope a 'hope of worms', according to Origen's reply *Against Celsus* (book 5; exact section needs verification). Bodily resurrection was the most offensive part of the message to educated Greeks, not a borrowed Greek idea.
19014: Between death and resurrection: Hades, paradise and Abraham's bosom
19015:
If the resurrection comes only on the last day, where are the dead now? The New Testament gives glimpses rather than a map. Jesus tells of a poor man carried to 'Abraham's bosom' while a rich man suffers in Hades, with a great gulf between them (Luke 16:19-31). He promises the dying thief, 'today you will be with me in paradise' (Luke 23:43). Paul speaks of departing to 'be with Christ' (Phil 1:23) and being 'at home with the Lord' (2 Cor 5:8). Revelation shows martyrs' souls under the heavenly altar, crying out and told to wait (Rev 6:9-11).

Most second- and third-century writers drew a picture from these texts: at death the soul goes to a place of waiting, often called Hades in the broad sense of 'the realm of the dead'. It is divided, with the righteous at rest and the wicked already in distress. Final reward and final punishment both wait for the resurrection and judgment. Irenaeus says souls go to an invisible place appointed by God and remain there until the resurrection. Tertullian, in *On the Soul*, describes all souls as held in the underworld until the last day, with the exception of the martyrs.

Justin Martyr even warned against people who say there is no resurrection and that souls are taken up to heaven at death, saying such people should not be counted as Christians. For him, skipping straight to heaven was a sign of denying the resurrection.

This 'intermediate state' teaching was not uniform. Some later writers, especially in the fourth century, spoke of the righteous being with Christ in heaven already, and the question of whether the saints see God before the resurrection was argued about for centuries (it was settled for Roman Catholics by *Benedictus Deus* in 1336).
19016: Christians still debate what Luke 16 teaches. Some read the story of the rich man and Lazarus as a window into the intermediate state. Others treat it as a parable using familiar Jewish imagery to make a moral point about wealth and repentance, not a literal description. Both readings are old.
19018:
One group was treated differently from the start: the martyrs. Revelation pictures those 'slain for the word of God' as already before God's altar (Rev 6:9-11), and Stephen, the first martyr, sees heaven opened and commits his spirit to Jesus as he dies (Acts 7:55-60).

Tertullian says plainly that while ordinary souls wait in the underworld, the martyrs go directly to paradise. Their deaths were described as a 'birthday' into true life. The Martyrdom of Polycarp, written soon after his death around 155, says the church at Smyrna gathered his bones and planned to meet each year on the day of his martyrdom to remember him and prepare others for their own trials. This is one of the earliest witnesses to the Christian cult of the saints.

The martyrs mattered because they made the resurrection hope visible. A person who died singing, rather than cursing, was public evidence that Christians really believed death had lost its sting (1 Cor 15:55). Over the following centuries, martyrs' tombs became places of prayer, and asking the martyrs to pray for the living became widespread.
19019: The practice of gathering at martyrs' tombs on the anniversary of their deaths is extra-biblical church tradition. It is attested by the mid-second century and grew into the calendar of saints' days.
19021:
Early Christians believed that between his death and resurrection Jesus went to the realm of the dead. Peter's sermon applies Psalm 16 to Jesus: God did not abandon him to Hades (Acts 2:27, Acts 2:31). Jesus speaks of the Son of Man being 'three days and three nights in the heart of the earth' (Matt 12:40). Two hard passages in 1 Peter speak of Christ preaching 'to the spirits in prison' and the gospel being preached 'to the dead' (1 Pet 3:18-20, 1 Pet 4:6). Ephesians says he 'descended into the lower parts of the earth' (Eph 4:8-10).

By the early second century, Ignatius of Antioch says the prophets, who were Christ's disciples in the Spirit, were raised by him when he came. Justin and Irenaeus both cite a saying they attribute to Jeremiah (it is not in our book of Jeremiah) about the Lord remembering his dead and going down to preach salvation to them. Later, the *Gospel of Nicodemus* told the story dramatically: Christ smashes the gates of Hades and leads out Adam, Eve and the righteous of old. This became the 'harrowing of hell' of medieval art and the central Easter icon of Eastern Orthodoxy.

The phrase 'he descended into hell' entered some Western creeds in the fourth century and became part of the Apostles' Creed. What it means has been debated. Some say Christ proclaimed victory, others that he freed Old Testament saints, others (following Calvin) that it describes his spiritual anguish on the cross, and some modern evangelicals (such as Wayne Grudem) argue the line should be dropped.
19022: Myth: 'The descent into hell is a late medieval invention.' Correction: the idea is attested by Ignatius (about 110) and Irenaeus (about 180). What came later was the dramatic storytelling and the creedal wording. What is genuinely debated is what 1 Peter 3:19 means, not whether early Christians believed in a descent.
